title: Phrygia
capsule: Phrygia was a kingdom of west-central Anatolia founded by Indo-European migrants who settled the region after the collapse of Hittite power around 1200 BCE, establishing their capital at Gordion on the Sakarya River. The dynasty reached its apex under King Midas (fl. c. 738–696 BCE), whose extraordinary wealth became legendary in Greek tradition, and who maintained diplomatic contact with Assyrian kings including Sargon II. Gordion was sacked by the Cimmerians around 696 BCE, an event Eusebius associates with Midas's death; this invasion effectively ended Phrygia's independence as a unified kingdom, though Phrygian culture and language persisted under Lydian and later Persian suzerainty. The Phrygians are noted for early iron-working, distinctive arts including the Phrygian cap, and their music, which influenced Greek musical modes.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Phrygian territory is attested through Assyrian royal annals, Greek literary sources, and archaeology at Gordion, but the kingdom's maximum extent and precise frontiers are uncertain, relying on inference from settlement patterns.
